questions.question: Trace the chain from self-sufficiency to trade, stating barter's four defects and the function of money that repairs each one.
questions.expected_answer: Self-sufficient households consumed only what their own hands produced, so every craft was practised badly under every roof. The agricultural revolution created surplus — output beyond the producers' needs — which freed hands for specialisation, and specialists must exchange. Barter's defects: the double coincidence of wants (a partner who has what you seek AND wants what you carry); indivisibility (half a sheep cannot buy a knife); no common measure of value (every pairing of goods needs its own haggled ratio); no store of value (food spoils, livestock wanders). Money repairs each: as a medium of exchange it dissolves the double coincidence; through divisibility any purchase size works; as a unit of account it puts prices on one measuring rod; as a store of value it lets wealth wait. Surviving commodity moneys were durable, divisible, portable and scarce.

questions.question: Name the tracks along which markets evolved, and the state's three historic entries with their motives.
questions.expected_answer: Markets deepened through specialisation (the division of labour multiplying output, feeding and fed by markets); trade and transport (roads, ships, railways widening the circle of customers); mercantile and commercial law (contracts, standard weights and measures, courts — personal trust becoming institutional trust between strangers); and evolving business forms (sole trader, partnership, then the company with ownership in shares — risk spread, capital gathered), with technological progress threading through all. The state entered by involvement in trade (regulating marketplaces, chartering companies, holding ports — because taxed trade financed power), by taxation (customs and levies growing into income and spending taxes, giving rulers a permanent stake in growth), and by financing infrastructure (roads, harbours, railways — enormously costly, benefiting all, repaying only indirectly: the textbook public investment). Each entry answers a market limitation.

questions.question: Set out industrialisation's four components, weigh its consequences on both sides, and describe South Africa's route into the industrial age.
questions.expected_answer: Components: manufacturing at factory scale (thousands where workshops made dozens, prices falling with volume); technological progress (knowledge cast into machines — looms, machine tools); the mobilisation of energy — the true rupture, water then steam then electricity and oil replacing muscle; and mechanisation absorbing tasks across farming, transport and industry. Gains: productivity leapt, goods cheapened, world markets knitted together. Costs and consequences: urbanisation as factories pulled workers into cities; two new classes — machine owners and machine operators — whose disputes became labour relations; and brutal conditions, child labour and pollution, the abuses that summoned labour law. South Africa industrialised through mining: diamonds then gold, railways flung inland, labour concentrated under the migrant labour system whose social costs persist — gains and costs braided together.
